question.prompt: A fair \(6\)-sided die is repeatedly rolled until an odd number appears. What is the probability that every even number appears at least once before the first occurrence of an odd number?

solutions.title: Record only new faces
solutions.explanation:
Repeating an even face does not change which even numbers have appeared. This suggests recording faces only when they first appear.

For this calculation, imagine continuing to roll even after the first odd number. A new face eventually appears with probability \(1\), and each unseen face is equally likely to be the next new face. Indeed, repeats merely delay that appearance, and swapping the labels of any two unseen faces leaves all roll probabilities unchanged.

Consequently, the ordered triples of the first three distinct faces are equally likely. There are
\[
6\cdot5\cdot4=120
\]
such triples: six choices for the first face, five for the second, and four for the third.

The desired event occurs exactly when these three faces are the three even numbers \(2,4,6\). If an odd face appears among them, the original process stops before all three evens have appeared. The favorable triples are the
\[
3\cdot2\cdot1=6
\]
orders of the even faces.

Therefore the probability is
\[
\frac{6}{120}=\boxed{\frac1{20}},
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).

solutions.title: Track progress after each roll
solutions.explanation:
Only the number of different even faces already seen matters for future success. This allows us to account for repeated rolls directly.

Let \(p_k\) be the probability of eventually succeeding when exactly \(k\) different even faces have appeared and no odd face has appeared. Future rolls are independent of the past, so the particular even faces do not matter. Once all three have appeared, success is secured, giving \(p_3=1\).

For \(k<3\), the next roll has three possible effects. With probability \(k/6\), it repeats an even face and leaves the situation unchanged. With probability \((3-k)/6\), it produces a new even face. With probability \(3/6\), it is odd and success becomes impossible. Thus
\[
p_k=\frac{k}{6}p_k+\frac{3-k}{6}p_{k+1}.
\]
Starting with \(p_3=1\), solve backward:
\[
\begin{aligned}
p_2&=\frac26p_2+\frac16
&&\Longrightarrow p_2=\frac14,\\
p_1&=\frac16p_1+\frac26\cdot\frac14
&&\Longrightarrow p_1=\frac1{10},\\
p_0&=\frac36\cdot\frac1{10}
&&=\frac1{20}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Initially no faces have appeared, so the requested probability is \(p_0=\boxed{\frac1{20}}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
